response_text:
Honestly, I think YTA here. You’ve been dating your girlfriend for just over a year and you already live together, which makes her feelings about trust and boundaries important in your relationship. You did invite her to the trip originally, and even rearranged to a date when she’d be away because she said she couldn’t go, which seems considerate. But after your third friend bailed, you should have immediately told your girlfriend the situation changed and checked in about her comfort level—especially since two-person overnight trips can get into sticky territory in monogamous relationships, no matter how innocent.

I get that everything is paid and it’s inconvenient to cancel, but your girlfriend has CLEAR misgivings about this and even framed it as a “date” and said she feels it crossed her boundaries and trust. It’s a red flag that she ended up setting some pretty extreme rules, like not initiating contact or requiring you to distance from your friend—but those rule requests don’t come from nowhere. You kept her in the dark about an important change, and now you’re prioritizing a trip over her emotional safety.

You asked for her input but then went ahead anyway, and that makes it feel like you’re dismissing her feelings. Even if you think her insecurities are unfounded, it’s your job as her partner to listen and reassure her instead of insisting on something she sees as a betrayal. That fact that you insist on the trip—especially after not communicating honestly—makes you TA in my opinion. Relationship trust and boundaries matter even if it means taking a hit to your weekend plans.

Absolutely NTA for refusing to cancel the trip. Here’s why:

You’ve been with your girlfriend for a year and even live together, which shows commitment. Originally, more people—including your girlfriend—were invited on this trip, which means it wasn’t planned as an intimate getaway with just this friend. Your girlfriend herself declined the invitation, and even specifically asked that you move the trip date to a weekend she’d be out of town. You and your friend went out of your way to rearrange plans to honor her request.

It was only after all this that a third friend dropped out, leaving you and your friend. Yes, you should have told your girlfriend about this right away, but I completely understand waiting for “the right time,” especially with people likely to have a strong reaction. But once you did tell her, her response was completely over the top. Not only did she demand you cancel and forbid you from going, she’s making unreasonable rules, like insisting you can’t hang out or even initiate contact with your friend and should distance yourself altogether.

Now, everything is already paid and booked. Given all this, I honestly don’t blame you one bit for not wanting to cancel.

Her accusations—that you being on a trip with one friend is somehow cheating or a “date”—really don’t add up, especially when you were up front about the invitation, rearranged the timing for her comfort, and have shown throughout your actions that you are committed and transparent.

The final straw is her threatening behavior: removing you from chat apps, refusing to have a real conversation, saying you should decide alone by email, but also saying breaking up isn’t an option. These are not the actions of someone dealing with a relationship issue in a healthy way. This seems way more about control than actual concern.

You shouldn’t have to end friendships or cancel harmless plans purely over someone else’s insecurities—especially after bending over backwards to accommodate them. The trust in a relationship has to go both ways.

NTA, and take your deserved break—you paid for it!

Honestly, OP, in this situation, YTA. I get that you and your 27F friend go way back and have been close since high school. I also understand the context—five years ago you had unrequited romantic feelings for her, drifted apart, but have since mended your friendship, which you now insist is 100% platonic from both sides.

Still, this isn’t just any friend: your girlfriend knows about the past, and now, after a third friend backed out, the trip's just you and the friend you once had feelings for, on a trip you used to take during uni “just the two of you”—a period when your romantic feelings were strongest.

I totally understand you tried hard to accommodate your girlfriend—changing the dates at her request, inviting her originally, and only confirming after she was unavailable. But honestly, all of this maybe should have been even more of a sign that extra sensitivity and reassurance was needed. When she expressed real discomfort and asked for you to cancel, instead of prioritizing the relationship, you went for an ultimatum—which, from her side, probably confirms her biggest fear: that you respect your friend and joint fun more than her boundary.

Even if your relationship with the friend is now platonic and you feel secure in that, relationships sometimes ask us to sacrifice for each other’s comfort and emotional safety. Everything being paid for already and all the rescheduling is annoying, but it’s not more valuable than your girlfriend genuinely feeling heard—especially knowing that this kind of situation is usually most important at the start of a relationship.

To me, the girlfriend’s reaction makes sense considering the history. To call her insecure or controlling over this honestly glosses over legitimate concerns. You chose your friend’s trip knowing the fallout it would bring. In the end, refusing to cancel the trip was the wrong call; if your girlfriend’s boundaries aren't ones you want to respect, maybe you *should* reconsider if the relationship is what you want, but you’re still TA for how it played out and for ignoring her reasonable discomfort.

No, I don't think you're in the wrong for refusing to cancel your trip with your friend over your girlfriend’s insecurities.

You’ve been with your girlfriend for just over a year and you already live together, which shows real commitment on your part. It also seems you went out of your way to be considerate by inviting her on the skating trip and even arranging the date so it wouldn’t conflict with her plans—at her request! You even tweaked your own and your friend’s schedules to make this work.

Yes, you and your friend did have some romantic feelings (on your end) years back, but the situation has changed: you drifted apart and recent history is all about repairing a valued friendship, with you making it very clear that your relationship is now purely platonic. She declined to come after all, and now it's just the two of you—and everything is already paid for.

What makes me think you’re NTA (“not the asshole”) is that your girlfriend previously had no visible insecurities about this friend, and suddenly turning possessive and demanding at the last minute seems more like controlling behavior than a true response to a real relationship threat. Especially since she “demanded” you cancel and “refused to allow” the trip, instead of talking openly. You had to even suggest you both reconsider the relationship, since healthy relationships require trust, not ultimatums.

In short, you did everything you could to make her comfortable and included, your intentions are straightforward, and your trip isn’t hurting anyone. Your girlfriend’s insecurity isn’t your job to fix if it crosses into controlling territory. Standing your ground here makes sense and is well within your rights as a partner and a person with a life outside your relationship.

Stay firm and have a great time skating!

Honestly, I can see where the tension is coming from, but *yes, YTA for refusing to cancel the trip with your friend over your girlfriend's insecurities.*

Here are the facts: You and your friend (27F) have been close since school and university, and yes, five years ago you had some one-sided romantic feelings. But that was a long time ago, you both drifted for a while, and now you've mended your friendship and it's strictly platonic. The skating trip was planned because you both enjoyed a similar trip back in university, and you even invited others—including your girlfriend—to join. When she declined, you *still* made an effort to accommodate her feelings by moving the trip date to a weekend when she'd be out of town; both you and your friend rearranged your plans for her. Now, with the third friend backing out, it’s just the two of you, but by then it’s already booked and paid.

Yet, your girlfriend is calling three days out of town "basically cheating," and laying down rules that you cannot initiate contact, hang out privately, and generally *distance* from a long-term, supposedly platonic friend. That's honestly unreasonable and controlling, especially after all the accommodations both you and your friend have made.

At the end of the day, your relationship with your friend is platonic, you’ve shown transparency and done a lot to address your girlfriend’s discomfort, but *you are not innocent here.* If your partner says something makes her feel like her trust is betrayed, a thoughtful response isn't just pushing forward anyway. Sometimes we need to prioritize our partner’s emotions—especially around old crushes—and be sensitive enough to postpone or replace a situation that is causing real distress. Going against her very clear boundaries *knowing* your history is dismissive of her trust and her role as your partner.

So, I get that the rules she’s imposing sound harsh. But, your refusal to consider her feelings and go through with the trip as planned—knowing her very real insecurities, which, justified or not, are *her reality right now*—makes it a bad move on your part. YTA.

Absolutely not, NTA. Here’s why:

First off, it sounds like you and your 27F friend have a strong, long-standing friendship — you’ve known each other since school and university, and yes, there was that period five years ago when you had feelings she didn’t reciprocate. You drifted, then made the effort to repair things, and that’s a testament to how much you both value each other. 

The skating trip was planned as a way to revisit fun you had in the past — like the similar trip you both did in university. Out of consideration, you actually invited other people (your girlfriend included), but she declined. Not only that, but at her request, you changed the trip dates to a weekend when she would be out of town — both you and your friend made accommodations! Then, the third planned participant canceled, but by then everything was booked and paid for, so it was just going to be you two. 

Now, after all these arrangements, your girlfriend claimed that this platonic, pre-planned and paid-for trip was basically a two-night, three-day "date" and went as far as to equate it to cheating. She even set “rules” for your friendship: no initiating contact, no hanging out privately, and a general mandate to distance yourself, regardless of your own comfort, your healthy friendship, or your assertive reassurances that those old romantic feelings are completely gone.

Given all this — the transparency, the thoughtful adjustments, and your own clarity about the platonic nature of the friendship — your girlfriend’s demands seem deeply unfair and controlling. Friendships are important, and you went above and beyond to include your girlfriend and address her insecurities, even reshuffling plans for her comfort. Expecting you to abandon a good friend — or a booked, vibrant trip — because of ungrounded insecurities crosses a line into unhealthy relationship dynamics.

Bottom line: You have a right to keep longstanding, platonic friends, especially when you’re not hiding anything. You shouldn’t have to cancel an important trip over unfounded accusations or strict “rules” about who you hang out with. Your actions have been respectful, honest, and conscientious — so no, you’re definitely not the asshole here.

Honestly, I think in this situation, YTA (you’re the asshole) for refusing to cancel the trip, and here’s why. You and your girlfriend (you’re 26F, she’s 30F) have been together for over a year and already live together – that’s a pretty serious relationship. I get that your 27F friend has been close to you for years, and it’s definitely important to keep longterm friendships in your life, but you yourself admit that five years ago you had unreciprocated romantic feelings for her. Even though you both drifted apart and only recently mended the friendship, that history can reasonably make a partner uneasy, even if nothing ever happened between you and your friend.

When you told your girlfriend it would just be the two of you on this trip, she asked you to cancel, and even went as far as setting rules: that you don’t initiate contact with this friend, don’t hang out privately, and distance yourself from the friendship. That’s definitely extreme and pretty controlling on her part, but you brushing all her worries aside and refusing to budge doesn’t show much empathy, either. Instead, you basically said her feelings were invalid and immediately jumped to reconsidering your whole relationship.

Your girlfriend’s next move was just as extreme—blocking you on chat apps and saying she wouldn’t consider a breakup, leaving you to decide alone and email the “result.” It’s clear there’s a load of trust and communication issues here, but in a healthy relationship you shouldn’t choose defiance over conversation, especially about something you KNOW triggers your partner’s insecurities, whether they’d mentioned it in the past or not.

Refusing to cancel the trip (in the immediate term) and prioritizing your friend SO flat-out, when you know your GF has honest insecurities (albeit escalating into controlling territory), is pretty cold. I honestly think you should have paused and had a proper, empathetic conversation to try to address both sides before making a decision. So, yes, YTA for outright refusing and not trying harder to resolve it—relationships demand empathy, especially when there are complex feelings around old friends and past crushes involved.

This doesn’t mean your girlfriend is handling things maturely by being controlling and demanding, but your approach was still TA. If you’re choosing a friend over engaging with your partner in good faith communication, what does that say about priorities in your relationship?

Here’s my take on this, as someone reading through all the facts:

First, OP (26F) has been dating her girlfriend (30F) for a little over a year and they live together. She also has a very close 27F friend who she’s known since school/university. Yes, there were unrequited feelings for the friend five years ago, but they drifted, then reconnected, and now it’s strictly friendship.

Now, when OP told her girlfriend about a trip that would just be the two of them, her girlfriend demanded she cancel, refusing to allow the trip because of her own insecurities. Not only that, the girlfriend set out really strict boundaries—basically forbidding OP from initiating contact, being alone with this friend, and insisting she distance herself overall. OP refused and instead pointed out how controlling and distrustful the behavior was, suggesting they reconsider the relationship. In response, her girlfriend kicked her off their chat apps and said she'd refuse to break up but left the burden of decision on OP.

Also key: before this, the girlfriend had never shown any such insecurity about this friend.

From my perspective, OP is absolutely *not* the asshole for refusing to cancel the trip. Friendships that predate your relationship deserve respect, and there is literally no indication of any current romantic feelings or danger here—just history, which both OP and her friend have moved past. What raised more red flags for me is the girlfriend’s insistence on “rules” that amount to controlling who OP is allowed to speak to and spend time with. Trust is everything in a relationship, and trying to isolate a partner out of insecurity is not healthy or acceptable behavior.

All in all, OP has every right to stand up for herself and draw lines at controlling, boundary-crossing demands. She’s handled it maturely by questioning if the relationship is worth pursuing under these conditions. The girlfriend’s ultimatums and controlling responses only underline who’s in the wrong. So no, OP is not the asshole here—she is defending her autonomy and friendships, and rightly so.

After really reading through everyone’s perspectives, I have to admit I can see a bit more nuance here than I originally did. I still lean toward thinking I’m not in the wrong for refusing to cancel the trip, given how much I tried to respect my girlfriend’s feelings—inviting her, rearranging for her schedule, communicating all the changes, and emphasizing the platonic nature of the friendship. However, I do see from several responses that maybe I was too focused on the “logic” of making things fair, and not enough on the bigger picture of trust and emotional safety: when your partner makes it clear (even unreasonably so) that they feel betrayed, it can require a different, more empathetic response than just doubling down on what’s “reasonable.” I also recognize that, for her, old wounds or trust issues might resurface even if it wasn’t obvious before, and that’s something important in a relationship—even if she expressed that in an arguably controlling way here. I still don’t believe her demand to cancel, cut off my friend, and accept rules about my social life is justified or healthy, but maybe I should’ve slowed down, acknowledged how deeply it bothered her, and offered more reassurance rather than letting it reach a breaking point. So, while I’m not convinced I’m “the asshole,” I can concede my own response may have been too inflexible. There were better options than just standing my ground, and next time I’ll try to balance my need for autonomy and old friendships with my partner’s need for comfort and trust.

After reading everyone else's input, I'm a bit more sympathetic to both sides, but honestly, I still lean toward my original YTA judgment—though maybe not as strongly as before. I acknowledged your girlfriend’s rules are controlling and definitely not healthy, which other people pointed out too, but several responses made me think more deeply about your role in communicating and handling her discomfort. People like View 2 and View 4 emphasized how, in serious relationships (especially where trust around past history is fragile), empathy and checking in really matter. While you made a solid effort to accommodate her from the start, the moment it became an intimate two-person trip—mirroring the circumstances when your crush was strongest—extra reassurance and discussion actually was warranted before you committed to not canceling. Yes, your partner’s unreasonable ultimatums complicate things, but your reaction of standing your ground and questioning the entire relationship in response didn’t really address any middle ground or show willingness to comfort. That said, people made convincing arguments (like View 5 and View 7) that no one should be forced to end valued friendships or submit to controlling behavior, particularly when you’ve communicated transparently and been considerate throughout. Honestly, I now see that it’s more of an ESH (everyone sucks here): your girlfriend for her controlling, unreasonable demands, but you too, for prioritizing defiance over open, empathetic discussion about something you *know* is a sticking point for her. Ultimately, your refusal to cancel without at least one more real, empathetic attempt at resolution looks like you’re choosing principle over partnership. So, while it’s complicated, I’m landing somewhere between my initial take and the strongest “NTA” responses: neither of you handled this in the healthiest way, and both sides missed opportunities to deal better with the issue.

After reading the new perspectives in the discussion, I appreciate the strong arguments in favor of standing up against controlling behavior and valuing long-term friendships, especially when you've shown transparency and gone out of your way to involve your partner and accommodate her. That being said, I still feel that, while your girlfriend’s rules and demands are extreme and over the line, your unwavering refusal came off as equally dismissive. It’s true that friends who predate relationships deserve respect, and I agree with those saying that being pushed to end such ties is unhealthy—but, I can also see how, given the specific history between you and your friend, a partner would need real reassurance when unexpected changes turn the trip into just you and someone you once had feelings for. At this point, I don’t think you’re the only one at fault; your girlfriend’s reaction worries me just as much. I believe you were wrong not to seize the chance for teamwork and open conversation about boundaries, but I now also think your girlfriend’s way of handling her fear is not fair or sustainable either. So my view has shifted—YTA, but a mild one, and mostly for communication breakdown rather than the refusal itself; but your girlfriend’s controlling reaction means the relationship’s issues run much deeper than one trip, and fault lies on both sides.

After reading everyone’s perspectives, I still side mostly with the idea that I’m not the asshole (NTA) for refusing to cancel the trip, but I do understand the other side better now. The key facts haven’t changed: this is a long-standing friend, not a new person, the original trip included other people, my girlfriend was invited but declined, and we specifically rescheduled the date for her convenience before the third person backed out and left just the two of us. I see now—thanks to others—how past romantic feelings, even if they were years ago and unreciprocated, could reasonably trigger discomfort for my girlfriend, and that more communication and reassurance might have been needed once the situation changed to an overnight trip with just us two. Some raised good points about prioritizing a partner’s need for emotional safety and about being extra considerate of their boundaries, particularly in monogamous relationships. However, I still think my refusal makes sense; having my girlfriend issue strict “rules” and attempt to limit my interactions crosses a healthy boundary for me, especially after I was transparent and accommodating at every turn. I sympathize with her reaction more now, but I also firmly believe standing up against controlling behavior—even if it springs from real insecurity—is important. I do wish we both handled the escalation more gently, and I see how a more empathetic conversation could’ve benefited us. Still, based on what happened, I remain convinced I’m not TA here, even as I acknowledge I could have done better on communication.

After reading everyone’s responses and really thinking through the details again, I still lean toward thinking YTA in this situation, but I do see the nuance more clearly now. Several folks pointed out just how much effort you actually put in—inviting your girlfriend, rearranging dates to suit her, being open about plans, and trying to accommodate her at each step. That transparency matters, and it’s fair to say she only made a big issue once the trip was very close, and proposed some harsh, frankly controlling “rules.” On the other hand, a few others echoed my concerns: regardless of past efforts, after the trip shifted to just you and an old friend you once liked—especially on a trip with a romantic-feeling history—your girlfriend had solid reasons to feel uneasy, and deserved real reassurance. I can now admit I might have underestimated how unreasonable her behavior became at the end: demanding, blocking you, then refusing to discuss anything except by email. Honestly, neither one of you handled the most intense moment as empathetically as you could have—your refusal reads cold, her demands and shutdown were over the top. So while I still think prioritizing the trip and failing to meet your girlfriend's emotional needs at the crucial moment leans YTA, I see now that she crossed boundary lines herself, and there’s no clear right or wrong here. In the end, it seems like there are mutual communication issues, with controlling behavior on her part but a lack of sensitivity on yours. I stand by seeing you as TA for not postponing or addressing it more collaboratively, but I’m beginning to think the whole outcome is just a sign you two might have incompatible needs.

Having read through everyone’s perspectives, I can see now that several people think I moved too quickly to defend my autonomy instead of first working harder to address my girlfriend’s discomfort and insecurities. I still believe it was not fair or healthy for my girlfriend to set strict, controlling rules and make immediate ultimatums about my friendships when there was little precedent for such jealousy—especially after I involved her in the planning and shifted my life around for her comfort. That being said, those pointing out that a truly healthy response might have included one more effort at calm, vulnerable conversation—with more acknowledgement of her position and maybe a short postponement or direct reminder of my commitment—make a fair point. I wish my girlfriend hadn’t jumped to extreme reactions and boundary-crossing demands, but I also see how my holding the line without inviting further dialogue or reassurance could seem dismissive, especially given the complicated history with my friend. So, while I still don’t believe I’m “TA” specifically for refusing to cancel plans I made transparently and with good intentions, I probably could have been a better, more empathetic partner by not letting things escalate to a showdown. Ultimately, refusing to cancel wasn’t wrong, but my communication could have been softer, and I can admit there’s no victory when the person you live with feels hurt or insecure, even if you’re ‘right.’ So I keep most of my view, but I now see my role as not quite blameless either.

Reading all the new perspectives, I still lean toward YTA, but maybe with a bit more understanding—especially after seeing how divided people are over what's controlling versus what's appropriate to expect in a relationship. I have to acknowledge you went further than many would to include your girlfriend (inviting her first, shifting the dates for her, and not hiding the trip), so I now can see why the “NTA” crowd feels you’ve been transparent and accommodating. On the other hand, the points about how your past feelings and the two-person, overnight aspect could create reasonable discomfort for a partner still stand. I think some of the more critical takes raise a valid point that, whether or not her rules escalated to controlling, your first responses shouldn’t have been ultimatums or quick defensiveness; a slower, softer conversation aimed at rebuilding reassurance (without just caving immediately or insisting she deal with it) might have had a different outcome. Even with all the effort you made, I still feel that totally refusing her concerns and proceeding anyway undermines relationship trust. So while the requests she made were harsh, you effectively chose your friend and the trip over seriously engaging with your girlfriend’s perspective—especially about past crushes—when things got tough. Bottom line: I now see it’s not black-and-white, but I still think YTA, although I appreciate the nuance and don’t think your girlfriend’s response was perfect either. Relationship communication is messy, but it comes down to both partners showing that when a real, emotional boundary crops up (right or wrong), it gets handled gently.

Looking over everyone’s feedback has definitely made me second-guess a few things, but I still mostly stand by my original assessment. A lot of you rightly pointed out that I handled the communication after the third friend dropped out a bit poorly—maybe I should have called my girlfriend right away and double-checked in light of the change, instead of just sharing it after the fact. I get that two-person, overnight trips can be touchy, especially with romantic history, and perhaps I could/should have signaled even more understanding or reassurance, or at least pushed for a real, calm talk before standing my ground so firmly. However, I still believe her reaction—to demand I cancel, lay down strict “control” rules, block me on apps, and assert a breakup wasn’t allowed—was disproportionate and unhealthy. Yes, partners deserve empathy and compromise, but there’s a line between sharing uncomfortable feelings and demanding control, and her approach seemed more about issuing ultimatums than working it out together. So, while I do admit I could have paused and tried for a softer, more open dialogue, in the end, I think refusing to cancel wasn’t wrong given all the earlier accommodations, transparency, and my intent. My girlfriend’s method of handling the conflict flags much bigger relationship issues to me. If she needed more reassurance, I wish she’d asked for it instead of moving straight to threats. So, my updated view: Maybe I could have communicated even better when plans changed, and if I’d tried even harder, some of this might’ve been avoided. Still, at bottom, standing up for my friendship and refusing to cancel was okay—her controlling response is not. So, mostly NTA, while admitting there were places I could’ve handled it better.

After considering the most recent feedback and really digesting people’s deeper takes—especially about that “breaking point moment” when my girlfriend became upset about the two-person overnight—I see my own perspective developing a little further. Most people seem to agree it was controlling for her to suddenly issue rules and demands, but I also notice a strong strain of opinion pointing to how, when her trust was explicitly shaken, I could have worked harder to show that I cared about her emotional safety and was invested enough in our relationship to at least pause and talk, rather than defaulting straight to “I’m not canceling.” Yes, my original accommodations—inviting, rescheduling, sharing info—matter a lot to me, and I still don’t feel it’s ever healthy to cave to ultimatums about friendships preexisting a romance. But reading how others have described middle grounds I didn’t try (like postponing briefly for one more conversation or being more vulnerable about reassuring her) makes me realize I probably did let my frustration “win out” instead of displaying real empathy in that crucial escalation. That said, I stand by thinking her demands were unhealthy and a major red flag—not just discomfort, but insistence on dictating rules, blocking me, and imposing breakups over disagreement. So overall, while I still don’t think I’m the asshole for not canceling in itself, I am now more clearly seeing that both of us let communication get lost to self-protection and stubbornness. I wish I’d handled things more gently when they got tense. At the end of the day, I keep my stance that refusing to cancel was justified, but I see now my approach could have shown more care—and the way we both responded exposed bigger incompatibilities in how we handle insecurity and conflict.

After taking in the new comments, especially the ones emphasizing both the context of your longstanding friendship and your efforts to include your girlfriend at each step, I still maintain that this is ultimately an ESH situation, though I’m not quite as firm as before in putting most blame on you. Reading others’ reasoning—including good points about how controlling your girlfriend’s response became, and how difficult it is to stay gentle when ultimatums get swapped for conversation—makes me even more convinced that both sides failed in key ways. I stand by the idea that, given the trip changed into a much more intimate context (overnight, past crush, just you two), it called for much more open and empathetic dialogue; just forging ahead on principle, even transparently, can feel cold or disrespectful in a committed relationship. At the same time, based on how harshly your girlfriend escalated—locking communication, laying down “rules,” and framing it as breakup-or-obedience—I’m more persuaded by those siding with your boundaries, especially after your prior acts of transparency. So bottom line, I haven’t changed my view much: both parties here let fear or defiance get in the way of actual trust-building, and neither handled the escalation as well as they could’ve. You aren’t an outright asshole for protecting a respectful friendship, but you missed a final opportunity to really demonstrate care when it might have mattered most. She crossed the line into controlling. I still think ESH, with an emphasis that the relationship may not stand unless both learn to move past self-protection and engage in honest, gentler conversation when the next tough dilemma arises.

Having thought more about everyone's latest input, I'm feeling more conflicted, but my perspective has shifted a little further toward the middle. Several people made strong points about how much effort and transparency you showed—inviting your girlfriend, rearranging dates, and making sure she was informed at every turn—which really does matter and makes the accusations of being inconsiderate less fair. Also, I see now that her demands crossed a line from genuine discomfort into outright control, which never tends to foster trust in a relationship. But at the same time, it's clear from other views—and I agree—that *something* more was needed, particularly as the trip suddenly became an intimate situation between you and a former crush. I admit now that simply refusing to cancel may not have addressed the emotional reality for your girlfriend, especially if there were preexisting insecurity or trust issues, and a more collaborative or reassuring approach could have been healthier. Ultimately, I still think your girlfriend’s way of handling this (with ultimatums and extreme "rules") was a red flag, but I also see that your response was too rigid, almost inviting escalation instead of understanding. So, I’m leaning closer now to ESH (everyone sucks here): I can’t say you’re just TA, as your actions came from reasonable motives and respect for boundaries, but you missed a crucial opportunity for empathy; meanwhile, her reaction—demanding you cut off a friendship in this way—was out of bounds. So, both of you played a part in letting the situation blow up, and neither responded in a way that feels truly healthy or fair.

Having reflected on the newest replies and the way people have evolved in their takes, I find my original view of “not the asshole” remains largely intact, though I recognize with more depth just how messy this was on both sides. The consistent facts don’t change: this was an established friend I’ve always been upfront about, I bent over backwards in planning (inviting my girlfriend, changing the dates, letting her know directly), and the shift to it being just two people really was outside my intent. I see more clearly now that the moment it became a close one-on-one trip with the person I’d once had feelings for, it did deserve a fresh, open check-in—not just assuming everything was still fine on the basis of past reassurance. Where my own approach could have been stronger is in offering more space for my girlfriend’s anxiety and not jumping immediately to draw my own hard lines, since everyone points out how fragile trust can be around these subjects. That said, her attempt to impose rules, demand cancellation, and respond by shutting me out still seems beyond what’s healthy in a partnership. After reading people’s nuanced arguments, I now admit my refusal was justified in the sense of not caving to insecurity-fueled, controlling demands, but my communication was likely too blunt and insufficiently empathetic given the very real stress this caused her. Next time, I’d want to try a more caring re-engagement, not just “standing my ground”—but I still don’t see myself as the asshole for keeping plans that were open, honest, and made in good faith. So, I’m keeping my basic view, but with added humility: my own lack of a reassuring response helped let things spiral, and in that sense, it’s clear neither of us handled the escalation as well as we should have.

After reading everyone else's thoughtful input, my view has shifted a bit, but I still ultimately land around a soft YTA—with the caveat that the situation is much more complex and there’s mutual fault here. I appreciate all the reminders that you made real efforts to include your girlfriend and that her demands absolutely crossed into controlling territory, which helps me see why so many people feel like refusing to cancel wasn't inherently wrong. However, I remain stuck on the way things played out after the trip changed to just you and the old friend: considering your girlfriend’s discomfort—especially with the history between you and your friend—a more empathetic approach, even just postponing or pausing for a real, calm talk, would have gone a long way. At the same time, your girlfriend escalated the “rules” and ultimatums so quickly that it undermined real dialogue and added to the toxicity.
